title: Parallel query processing
lead: Shared-resource architectures, data placement, parallel operators and distributed join plans.

sections.title: Architectures and levels of parallelism
sections.html:
Shared-memory processors access a common address space; shared-disk nodes have private memory but common storage; shared-nothing nodes have private CPU, memory and storage and communicate by network. Each architecture changes coordination and bottlenecks.

Inter-query parallelism runs different queries concurrently. Intra-query parallelism divides one query: inter-operator parallelism overlaps different operators, while intra-operator parallelism divides one operator’s work across partitions.

Pipeline parallelism is constrained by blocking operators. Independent branches can run in parallel, and partition-parallel scans or joins can process disjoint work simultaneously. The logical query answer must remain unchanged.

PDF pp. 1–11

sections.title: Partitioning and replication
sections.html:
Horizontal partitioning assigns whole tuples to disjoint partitions. Round-robin spreads tuples without key locality. Hash partitioning colocates equal partition keys. Range partitioning assigns key intervals and supports range-based pruning.

Replication stores additional copies of a partition or an entire table. It can improve availability and local reads but introduces update-propagation and consistency work. Replication and partitioning are independent design choices.

Data transparency hides placement from applications: the same logical query should return the same answer despite partitioning or replication. The optimiser still needs placement metadata to determine local work and communication.

PDF pp. 12–19

sections.title: Parallel scans, hashing and sorting
sections.html:
A parallel scan reads local partitions and combines their results. A predicate on the partition key can prune irrelevant partitions; a lookup without usable placement information may need broadcasting.

Parallel hash join partitions both inputs by the same join-key function, then performs local joins. Matching keys must reach the same node. Parallel sorting assigns nonoverlapping key ranges to nodes and sorts locally; global ordering requires combining ranges in order.

Parallel sort-merge join likewise uses compatible ranges on both inputs. Data exchange is part of the physical plan, not an optional step that can be omitted from cost estimates.

PDF pp. 20–26

sections.title: Four distributed join layouts
sections.html:
If one input is replicated, each node joins its disjoint local partition of the other input with that replica. If both inputs are compatibly partitioned on the join key, local joins require no repartitioning.

If placement is incompatible and one input is small, broadcast the small input to all join workers. If neither input is suitably placed or cheap to replicate, repartition both on the join key and join corresponding partitions.

Each plan must avoid duplicate result production when replicas are present. Its cost includes bytes moved, local join work, memory needs and collecting the output. The source illustrates these scenarios across successive node-placement figures.

PDF pp. 27–42

sections.title: Network cost and skew
sections.html:
Predicate and projection pushdown, join ordering and access-method selection remain relevant in a distributed plan. They also reduce bytes sent before an exchange.

Parallel latency follows the critical path rather than the sum of all worker times. If workers finish in 500 ms and 300 ms, that stage completes after 500 ms before accounting for other dependent stages.

Skew can concentrate tuples or expensive keys on one worker, making extra workers ineffective. The optimiser must consider placement, network transfer, dependencies and the slowest partition alongside local I/O and CPU work.

PDF pp. 43–45

quiz.question: Workers take 4, 5, 5, and 15 seconds in one parallel phase. What is the lower bound on the phase duration?
quiz.explanation: The phase must wait for its slowest worker. Coordination and network overhead may increase the total duration further.

source.summary: Lecture 26 compares resource-sharing architectures, levels of parallelism, partitioning and replication, parallel scans, sorts, and joins, and cost models that account for network traffic and skew.
